title: How long is a soccer game? Why the clock keeps going
description: A soccer match has two 45-minute halves, but it rarely ends at 90 on the clock. Here is how added time differs from extra time, with one simple example.

sections.title: Ninety minutes, with a little more to come
sections.html:
A standard adult football (soccer) match has two 45-minute halves: 90 minutes of regulation time, plus added time for stoppages. The half-time break is separate and must not exceed 15 minutes. Shorter playing periods can be agreed beforehand where competition rules allow.

So “90 minutes” is not a promise that you will be back in the kitchen exactly an hour and a half after kick-off.

sections.title: The clock keeps going; lost time is allowed for
sections.html:
The referee allows time in each half for delays such as injuries, substitutions, goal celebrations and video reviews. IFAB Law 7 sets out the rule.

That allowance is often called stoppage time or added time. It accounts for time lost during the half.

sections.title: What does +5 actually mean?
sections.html:
The board shows the minimum additional time. The referee can increase it, but cannot reduce it.

Imagine the board shows +5 at 90 minutes. You can expect at least five more minutes. If another delay follows, the whistle need not arrive at exactly 95:00. The board is not a countdown alarm.

sections.title: Added time is not extra time
sections.html:
Extra time is a separate way to settle a drawn match when competition rules require a winner. IFAB Law 10 permits two equal periods of up to 15 minutes each. A competition may instead use a penalty shoot-out; that happens after the match has ended.

Not every draw gets extra time. Check the competition’s format. For another match-day mystery, read our simple guide to offside.
